title: Adaptive inference and function vectors in deep transformers

paper.title: Adaptive inference and function vectors in deep transformers
paper.abstract:
Abstract Transformers are widely used as a general-purpose substrate for learning complex correlations between a large collection of coupled variables, but their internal mechanisms have remained mysterious.
We introduce a theory of a deep transformer as a mean-field interacting system that implements distributed inference, subject to constraints on communication, locality and depth. We show that such a system can exploit internal state representations (‘function vectors’) to infer a latent context variable at increasingly finer scales over its layers.
In an in-context regression task, the theory predicts a non-trivial relationship between non-Gaussian, hierarchical structure in the latent context variable, and transformer depth. Predictions are tested using constrained linear attention transformers and demonstrate adaptive inference in deep architectures. Feedforward blocks and depth enable transformers to implement a much richer class of in-context learning algorithms than previously described.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: In statistical physics, one is interested in describing the joint distribution of a large collection of coupled random variables, P ⁡ ( 𝒛 1 , 𝒛 2 , … , 𝒛 N ) P(\bm{z}_{1},\bm{z}_{2},\dots,\bm{z}_{N}) . Many techniques have been developed to estimate this distribution from data, often requiring simplifying ansätze that allow for efficient inference. In recent years, a complementary empirical paradigm has proved remarkably successful. Rather than specifying the form of the effective interactions by hand, one trains a flexible architecture on large and diverse datasets using relatively simple optimization rules [ 35 , 33 , 19 ] . The transformer architecture has emerged as one such general-purpose substrate [ 49 , 38 , 28 , 47 , 13 , 30 ] , and now forms the basis of foundation models in many domains, including vision [ 16 , 40 , 29 ] , speech [ 4 , 26 , 41 ] , materials design [ 39 ] and molecule generation [ 27 , 5 , 12 , 51 ] . The flexibility of a transformer arises from two operations that are repeated across layers. The first is a global interaction, mediated by self-attention, in which each vector (or ‘token’) in the input sequence extracts information from other tokens through learned interaction maps. The second is a local nonlinear computation, usually implemented as a multi-layer perceptron (MLP), which acts independently and identically on each vector. Once its parameters are optimized, a transformer can adapt its predictions to a novel sequence or dataset in a single forward pass, without further updates to its parameters. This phenomenon, called in-context learning, suggests that the transformer has learned a generic procedure for inferring structure from context [ 9 , 34 ] . In-context learning has served as a paradigm for probing the internal mechanisms of transformers [ 52 , 18 , 3 , 6 ] . Based on empirical work, we know that transformers implement in-context learning using at least two motifs: (1) attention circuits that implement specific algorithmic operations, such as copying [ 34 , 42 , 7 ] or gradient descent [ 36 , 2 , 37 , 55 ] , and (2) by forming function vectors [ 48 , 24 , 25 , 53 ] , which are internal representations of the function or task the model deems is being solved. While recent theoretical efforts have shed light on the former class of mechanisms [ 42 , 31 , 2 , 36 , 55 , 56 , 23 , 21 ] , the transformer circuits that enable the latter have remained unclear. First identified in large language models [ 24 , 48 ] , function (or task) vectors are consistently found in the middle layers of billion-parameter models of different families, suggesting a common underlying principle that favors this organization. In recent empirical work [ 22 ] , we find that, in contrast to pure attention-based circuits, leveraging function vectors necessarily entails a multi-layer interaction between the attention and MLP blocks. These observations offer a path towards a more general theory of in-context learning in transformers, which we now explore. In this Letter, we propose a theory of collective computation mediated by function vectors in multi-layer (deep) transformers. The theory is built on the hypothesis that a transformer, once optimized on a large dataset, implements distributed inference over a set of vectorized tokens, subject to architectural constraints on communication, locality, and depth. The theory makes specific predictions about the role of non-Gaussianity in latent context variables, and the value offered by depth and MLP blocks. These predictions are confirmed in numerical experiments with constrained linear attention transformers. Figure 1: Model schematic. Information about a latent contextual variable 𝜽 \bm{\theta} implicit in the context 𝒵 N \mathcal{Z}_{N} is compressed through L L rounds of interaction into a function vector 𝚽 L \bm{\Phi}_{L} , which is subsequently used by a query for prediction (through a decoder; blue square). At every layer ℓ \ell , the local nonlinearity (red square) uses ( 𝒙 i , 𝒚 i ) (\bm{x}_{i},\bm{y}_{i}) and the intermediate function vector 𝚽 ℓ \bm{\Phi}_{\ell} to construct an embedding function 𝝀 ℓ + 1 ​ ( 𝒙 i , 𝒚 i , 𝚽 ℓ ) \bm{\lambda}_{\ell+1}(\bm{x}_{i},\bm{y}_{i},\bm{\Phi}_{\ell}) . The embedding of the N N contextual tokens is pooled (grey rectangle) to form a d d -dimensional statistic 𝝋 ℓ + 1 \bm{\varphi}_{\ell+1} . This pooled statistic is concatenated: 𝚽 ℓ + 1 = 𝚽 ℓ ⊕ 𝝋 ℓ + 1 \bm{\Phi}_{\ell+1}=\bm{\Phi}_{\ell}\oplus\bm{\varphi}_{\ell+1} .

sections.text: We begin by considering a standard in-context learning paradigm [ 18 , 2 , 55 , 31 ] . We wish to learn the joint distribution of a collection of N N random variables (‘tokens’), 𝒵 N = { 𝒛 1 , 𝒛 2 , … , 𝒛 N } \mathcal{Z}_{N}=\{\bm{z}_{1},\bm{z}_{2},\dots,\bm{z}_{N}\} . The tokens are coupled by a latent context variable 𝜽 \bm{\theta} , drawn from ρ 0 ​ ( 𝜽 ) \rho_{0}(\bm{\theta}) . That is, P ⁡ ( { 𝒛 i } ) = ∫ d ​ 𝜽 ​ ρ 0 ​ ( 𝜽 ) ​ ∏ i p ⁡ ( 𝒛 i | 𝜽 ) P(\{\bm{z}_{i}\})=\int d\bm{\theta}\rho_{0}(\bm{\theta})\prod_{i}p(\bm{z}_{i}|\bm{\theta}) . The model is trained to predict a masked out component in a separate query token using the context 𝒵 N \mathcal{Z}_{N} . Specifically, each token is split into two components, 𝒛 = ( 𝒙 , 𝒚 ) \bm{z}=(\bm{x},\bm{y}) , where p ⁡ ( 𝒛 | 𝜽 ) = q ⁡ ( 𝒙 | 𝜽 ) ​ π ​ ( 𝒚 | 𝒙 , 𝜽 ) p(\bm{z}|\bm{\theta})=q(\bm{x}|\bm{\theta})\pi(\bm{y}|\bm{x},\bm{\theta}) . Given 𝒵 N \mathcal{Z}_{N} and an independently drawn query token 𝒙 \bm{x} from the same 𝜽 \bm{\theta} , the model is trained to construct a predictive distribution π ^ ​ ( 𝒚 | 𝒙 , 𝒵 N ) ≈ π ⁡ ( 𝒚 | 𝒙 , 𝜽 ) \hat{\pi}(\bm{y}|\bm{x},\mathcal{Z}_{N})\approx\pi(\bm{y}|\bm{x},\bm{\theta}) by optimizing a prediction loss ⟨ ℒ ⁡ ( π ^ ) ⟩ \langle\mathcal{L}(\hat{\pi})\rangle . ℒ \mathcal{L} is typically a cross-entropy loss or a mean-squared-error loss, and the expectation is over samples of 𝜽 ∼ ρ 0 \bm{\theta}\sim\rho_{0} , a new set of contextual tokens 𝒵 N \mathcal{Z}_{N} given 𝜽 \bm{\theta} , and a new query 𝒙 ∼ q ( . | 𝜽 ) \bm{x}\sim q(.|\bm{\theta}) . We introduce a model for distributed Bayesian inference mediated by mean-field interactions between a collection of tokens (Figure 1 ). The model consists of L L layers, where each layer is a round of interactions between tokens and a local nonlinear operation that processes each token separately. Importantly, interactions are constrained to a channel dimension d d . We assume a common masking scheme where the context tokens cannot interact with the query, whereas the query can access the shared communication channel among the context tokens. We first show how this model can implement adaptive inference and later map this model to a transformer architecture with a simplified attention operation. First, suppose L = 1 L=1 . Since 𝜽 \bm{\theta} is a shared variable, the tokens should exchange information to perform inference. We assume interactions are mediated through a shared pool: 𝝋 1 = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N 𝝀 1 ​ ( 𝒛 i ) , \displaystyle\bm{\varphi}_{1}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bm{\lambda}_{1}(\bm{z}_{i}), (1) where 𝝀 1 \bm{\lambda}_{1} is a d d -dimensional nonlinear embedding of each token and 𝝋 1 \bm{\varphi}_{1} is a globally accessible statistic that carries information about 𝜽 \bm{\theta} . The query 𝒙 \bm{x} can access 𝝋 1 \bm{\varphi}_{1} to form a posterior ρ ⁡ ( 𝜽 | 𝒙 , 𝝋 1 ) \rho(\bm{\theta}|\bm{x},\bm{\varphi}_{1}) and thereby generate a predictive distribution π ^ ​ ( 𝒚 | 𝒙 , 𝒵 N ) = ∫ d ​ 𝜽 ​ ρ ​ ( 𝜽 | 𝒙 , 𝝋 1 ) ​ π ​ ( 𝒚 | 𝒙 , 𝜽 ) \hat{\pi}(\bm{y}|\bm{x},\mathcal{Z}_{N})=\int d\bm{\theta}\rho(\bm{\theta}|\bm{x},\bm{\varphi}_{1})\pi(\bm{y}|\bm{x},\bm{\theta}) . Since information about the context is shared to the query entirely through 𝝋 1 \bm{\varphi}_{1} , we call 𝝋 1 \bm{\varphi}_{1} the function vector corresponding to the context 𝒵 N \mathcal{Z}_{N} . This definition of a function vector aligns with empirically motivated definitions of function/task vectors [ 48 , 24 , 22 ] : an internal representation of a model is deemed a function vector if patching in the function vector from context 𝒵 N \mathcal{Z}_{N} into a different context 𝒵 N ′ \mathcal{Z}^{\prime}_{N} produces a response to a novel query 𝒙 \bm{x} in context 𝒵 N ′ \mathcal{Z}^{\prime}_{N} that aligns with context 𝒵 N \mathcal{Z}_{N} . In other words, a function vector is a compact summary of the information in the context for predicting the target 𝒚 \bm{y} for any novel query 𝒙 \bm{x} . Now, suppose L ≥ 1 L\geq 1 . Let us say we want to adaptively select the embedding at the next layer 𝝀 ℓ + 1 \bm{\lambda}_{\ell+1} to optimize the final prediction loss after L L rounds of interaction. At layer ℓ + 1 \ell+1 , the model then appends the corresponding statistic 𝝋 ℓ + 1 \bm{\varphi}_{\ell+1} to the state, so that 𝚽 ℓ + 1 = 𝚽 ℓ ⊕ 𝝋 ℓ + 1 \bm{\Phi}_{\ell+1}=\bm{\Phi}_{\ell}\oplus\bm{\varphi}_{\ell+1} . sections.heading: III Discussion
sections.text: A prominent view is that in-context learning emulates Bayesian inference over a latent context variable [ 33 , 52 ] , whereas mechanistic studies of in-context linear regression have shown how attention circuits can implement algorithms such as preconditioned gradient descent [ 2 , 36 , 55 ] . We make progress towards reconciling the gap between these two perspectives by showing that deep transformers can implement Bayesian inference as a distributed, adaptive, layerwise procedure: function vectors act as compressed state variables, MLP blocks choose which statistic should be measured next, and attention pools that statistic across the context. This mechanism places function vectors [ 48 , 24 , 25 , 53 , 22 ] in a circuit-level framework and shows that depth and MLP blocks enable a much richer class of in-context learning algorithms than preconditioned gradient descent. The theory ignores a key element of typical transformer architectures, softmax attention, which allows tokens to retrieve information from specific tokens in the context at the expense of a quadratic scaling of computation with context size [ 32 ] . Softmax attention is analogous to an implementation of a key-value memory over the context [ 8 , 46 ] , and plays an important role in implementing attention-based circuit computations for in-context learning [ 34 , 7 , 42 , 22 ] . The pooling-based operation in our theory is linear in context size while respecting exchangeability [ 15 , 54 , 17 ] , namely, permutation invariance of the data conditional on the latent context variable, and thus may be sufficient to implement in-context learning in such scenarios. Recent analyses that treat self-attention as an interacting-particle system similarly emphasize a collective description of token dynamics, but focus on the evolution of the empirical distribution of token representations and the emergence of clustering or metastable macroscopic states [ 20 , 10 , 44 ] . In a complementary direction, in-context denoising identifies regimes in which attention implements a context-dependent associative-memory or score-like denoising update [ 46 , 43 ] . Integrating these perspectives with the constrained Bayesian framework developed here may clarify how transformers combine local memory retrieval with adaptive inference using feedforward blocks.

sections.heading: VI.5 Relation to linear attention transformers
sections.text: The architecture in Eq. ( 6 ) can be understood as a constrained linear attention transformer which isolates low-dimensional communication between tokens. Here, we briefly explain how it arises from a standard linear attention update. Consider a residual stream activation 𝒖 i , ℓ ∈ ℝ D \bm{u}_{i,\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} for token i i at layer ℓ \ell . The standard linear attention update is written as 𝒖 i , ℓ + 1 = 𝒖 i , ℓ + 𝑶 ℓ ​ [ ( 1 N ​ ∑ j = 1 N ( 𝑽 ℓ ​ 𝒖 j , ℓ ) ​ ( 𝑲 ℓ ​ 𝒖 j , ℓ ) ⊤ ) ​ 𝑸 ℓ ​ 𝒖 i , ℓ ] \bm{u}_{i,\ell+1}=\bm{u}_{i,\ell}+\bm{O}_{\ell}\quantity[\qty(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N (\bm{V}_\ell\bm{u}_{j,\ell})(\bm{K}_\ell\bm{u}_{j,\ell})^\top)\bm{Q}_\ell\bu_{i,\ell}] (25) where 𝑸 ℓ , 𝑲 ℓ , 𝑽 ℓ , 𝑶 ℓ \bm{Q}_{\ell},\bm{K}_{\ell},\bm{V}_{\ell},\bm{O}_{\ell} are learned matrices. We now restrict the model to d d independent attention heads with query/key dimension 1 each, as opposed to a single attention head with query/key dimension d d . In this case, each attention head communicates a single scalar channel, and the linear attention update becomes 𝒖 i , ℓ + 1 \displaystyle\bm{u}_{i,\ell+1} = 𝒖 i , ℓ + 𝑶 ℓ ​ [ 𝝋 ℓ ⊙ ( 𝑸 ℓ ​ 𝒖 i , ℓ ) ] , \displaystyle=\bm{u}_{i,\ell}+\bm{O}_{\ell}\quantity[\bvp{\ell} \odot(\bm{Q}_\ell\bu_{i,\ell})], (26) 𝝋 ℓ \displaystyle\bm{\varphi}_{\ell} = 1 N ​ ∑ j = 1 N ( 𝑽 ℓ ​ 𝒖 j , ℓ ) ⊙ ( 𝑲 ℓ ​ 𝒖 j , ℓ ) , \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}(\bm{V}_{\ell}\bm{u}_{j,\ell})\odot(\bm{K}_{\ell}\bm{u}_{j,\ell}), (27) where 𝝋 ℓ \bm{\varphi}_{\ell} is the pooled key-value statistic that acts as a global context-dependent representation of the present information. The elementwise product preserves all d d communication channels independently, in contrast to the standard matrix-vector contraction which mixes the channels. We next partition the residual stream into two as 𝒖 i , ℓ = 𝒛 i ⊕ 𝒑 ℓ , \bm{u}_{i,\ell}=\bm{z}_{i}\oplus\bm{p}_{\ell}, (28) where 𝒛 i = ( 𝒙 i , 𝒚 i ) \bm{z}_{i}=(\bm{x}_{i},\bm{y}_{i}) stores the contextual token information and 𝒑 ℓ \bm{p}_{\ell} is a shared internal workspace that evolves across layers. The workspace 𝒑 ℓ \bm{p}_{\ell} is identical across all tokens and acts as the state variable which stores a representation of the accumulated information about the context. Only 𝒑 ℓ \bm{p}_{\ell} is updated across layers, while the token representation 𝒛 i \bm{z}_{i} remains fixed. Once this separation is made, the useful information for the regression task is contained entirely in 𝒛 i \bm{z}_{i} , while 𝒑 ℓ \bm{p}_{\ell} controls how information is processed and routed across layers. The theory developed in the main text predicts that later measurements should depend on information acquired in earlier layers. To implement this adaptive measurement strategy, we let the key matrix 𝑲 ℓ \bm{K}_{\ell} depend on the workspace 𝑲 ℓ = ϕ ¯ ℓ ​ ( 𝒑 ¯ ℓ ) , \bm{K}_{\ell}=\bar{\bm{\phi}}_{\ell}(\bar{\bm{p}}_{\ell}), (29) where ϕ ¯ ℓ \bar{\bm{\phi}}_{\ell} is a feedforward block (MLP). Thus, the current internal state determines which measurement is performed at the next layer. The update to the workspace thus reads 𝒑 ℓ + 1 = 𝒑 ℓ + 𝑶 ℓ ​ [ 𝝋 ℓ ⊙ ( 𝑸 ℓ ​ 𝒑 ℓ ) ] . \bm{p}_{\ell+1}=\bm{p}_{\ell}+\bm{O}_{\ell}\quantity[\bvp{\ell}\odot(\bm{Q}_\ell\bm{p}_\ell)]. (30) We finally include a factor of 1 / d 1/\sqrt{d} as a form of width normalization for the residual update, ensuring that the magnitude of the communicated signal remains 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 ) \mathcal{O}(1) as the channel dimension d d is varied, leading to the form of Eq. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2606.16694v1 [cs.LG] 15 Jun 2026 Adaptive inference and function vectors in deep transformers Ravin Raj Affiliation: Joseph Henry Laboratories of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, USA Gautam Reddy Email: greddy@princeton.edu Affiliation: Joseph Henry Laboratories of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, USA Abstract Transformers are widely used as a general-purpose substrate for learning complex correlations between a large collection of coupled variables, but their internal mechanisms have remained mysterious. We introduce a theory of a deep transformer as a mean-field interacting system that implements distributed inference, subject to constraints on communication, locality and depth. We show that such a system can exploit internal state representations (‘function vectors’) to infer a latent context variable at increasingly finer scales over its layers. In an in-context regression task, the theory predicts a non-trivial relationship between non-Gaussian, hierarchical structure in the latent context variable, and transformer depth. Predictions are tested using constrained linear attention transformers and demonstrate adaptive inference in deep architectures. Feedforward blocks and depth enable transformers to implement a much richer class of in-context learning algorithms than previously described. I Introduction In statistical physics, one is interested in describing the joint distribution of a large collection of coupled random variables, P ⁡ ( 𝒛 1 , 𝒛 2 , … , 𝒛 N ) P(\bm{z}_{1},\bm{z}_{2},\dots,\bm{z}_{N}) . Many techniques have been developed to estimate this distribution from data, often requiring simplifying ansätze that allow for efficient inference. In recent years, a complementary empirical paradigm has proved remarkably successful. Rather than specifying the form of the effective interactions by hand, one trains a flexible architecture on large and diverse datasets using relatively simple optimization rules [ 35 , 33 , 19 ] . The transformer architecture has emerged as one such general-purpose substrate [ 49 , 38 , 28 , 47 , 13 , 30 ] , and now forms the basis of foundation models in many domains, including vision [ 16 , 40 , 29 ] , speech [ 4 , 26 , 41 ] , materials design [ 39 ] and molecule generation [ 27 , 5 , 12 , 51 ] . The flexibility of a transformer arises from two operations that are repeated across layers. The first is a global interaction, mediated by self-attention, in which each vector (or ‘token’) in the input sequence extracts information from other tokens through learned interaction maps. The second is a local nonlinear computation, usually implemented as a multi-layer perceptron (MLP), which acts independently and identically on each vector. Once its parameters are optimized, a transformer can adapt its predictions to a novel sequence or dataset in a single forward pass, without further updates to its parameters. This phenomenon, called in-context learning, suggests that the transformer has learned a generic procedure for inferring structure from context [ 9 , 34 ] . In-context learning has served as a paradigm for probing the internal mechanisms of transformers [ 52 , 18 , 3 , 6 ] . Based on empirical work, we know that transformers implement in-context learning using at least two motifs: (1) attention circuits that implement specific algorithmic operations, such as copying [ 34 , 42 , 7 ] or gradient descent [ 36 , 2 , 37 , 55 ] , and (2) by forming function vectors [ 48 , 24 , 25 , 53 ] , which are internal representations of the function or task the model deems is being solved. While recent theoretical efforts have shed light on the former class of mechanisms [ 42 , 31 , 2 , 36 , 55 , 56 , 23 , 21 ] , the transformer circuits that enable the latter have remained unclear. First identified in large language models [ 24 , 48 ] , function (or task) vectors are consistently found in the middle layers of billion-parameter models of different families, suggesting a common underlying principle that favors this organization. In recent empirical work [ 22 ] , we find that, in contrast to pure attention-based circuits, leveraging function vectors necessarily entails a multi-layer interaction between the attention and MLP blocks. These observations offer a path towards a more general theory of in-context learning in transformers, which we now explore. In this Letter, we propose a theory of collective computation mediated by function vectors in multi-layer (deep) transformers. The theory is built on the hypothesis that a transformer, once optimized on a large dataset, implements distributed inference over a set of vectorized tokens, subject to architectural constraints on communication, locality, and depth. The theory makes specific predictions about the role of non-Gaussianity in latent context variables, and the value offered by depth and MLP blocks. III Discussion A prominent view is that in-context learning emulates Bayesian inference over a latent context variable [ 33 , 52 ] , whereas mechanistic studies of in-context linear regression have shown how attention circuits can implement algorithms such as preconditioned gradient descent [ 2 , 36 , 55 ] . We make progress towards reconciling the gap between these two perspectives by showing that deep transformers can implement Bayesian inference as a distributed, adaptive, layerwise procedure: function vectors act as compressed state variables, MLP blocks choose which statistic should be measured next, and attention pools that statistic across the context. This mechanism places function vectors [ 48 , 24 , 25 , 53 , 22 ] in a circuit-level framework and shows that depth and MLP blocks enable a much richer class of in-context learning algorithms than preconditioned gradient descent. The theory ignores a key element of typical transformer architectures, softmax attention, which allows tokens to retrieve information from specific tokens in the context at the expense of a quadratic scaling of computation with context size [ 32 ] . Softmax attention is analogous to an implementation of a key-value memory over the context [ 8 , 46 ] , and plays an important role in implementing attention-based circuit computations for in-context learning [ 34 , 7 , 42 , 22 ] . The pooling-based operation in our theory is linear in context size while respecting exchangeability [ 15 , 54 , 17 ] , namely, permutation invariance of the data conditional on the latent context variable, and thus may be sufficient to implement in-context learning in such scenarios. Recent analyses that treat self-attention as an interacting-particle system similarly emphasize a collective description of token dynamics, but focus on the evolution of the empirical distribution of token representations and the emergence of clustering or metastable macroscopic states [ 20 , 10 , 44 ] . In a complementary direction, in-context denoising identifies regimes in which attention implements a context-dependent associative-memory or score-like denoising update [ 46 , 43 ] . Integrating these perspectives with the constrained Bayesian framework developed here may clarify how transformers combine local memory retrieval with adaptive inference using feedforward blocks.
